name: ka
goal: Make a simple statement about something, and comment on it the way Burmese speakers actually open small talk — through the weather.

lines: မင်္ဂလာပါ။
မင်္ဂလာပါ။ ပူတယ်နော်။
ဟုတ်ကဲ့၊ ပူပါတယ်။

vocab: ဘယ်သွားမလဲ
"where are you headed?" — real street greeting
"have you eaten yet?" — real street greeting
to be all right / it's fine

grammar.title: -deh — the statement ending
grammar.explain: Every plain Burmese statement ends in -deh (or -teh after a syllable ending in -q). It's the neutral, all-purpose "is/does" ending — there's no separate word for "to be."

grammar.title: -naw — inviting agreement
grammar.explain: Add -naw to the end of a -deh statement to turn it into a tag question — like English "...isn't it?" Commenting on the weather this way is one of the most common ways to open a conversation in Burmese, the same way English speakers open with "nice day, huh?"
examples: ပူတယ်နော်။

write: The anchor loop of the whole script. Start at the top, curve down and left, close the loop back where you started — one continuous stroke.
culture: Notice the receptionist opens with Mingalar-ba — that's genuine, but it's not what two Burmese friends say passing each other on the street. Mingalar-ba is a 20th-century coinage, popularized through schools and radio, and today it lives mainly in formal, service, or foreigner-facing settings — exactly this one. On the street, people mostly skip "hello" entirely and ask a real question instead: Beh thwa-mha-lé? ("Where are you headed?") or Hta-min sa-pi-bi-la? ("Have you eaten yet?") — the same way "how's it going" in English isn't really asking about your wellbeing. Nobody expects a detailed answer to either; "just around" or "not yet" closes the loop fine.

name: hka
goal: Pay someone a compliment and receive one — the polite way, with -ba-/-pa-.

lines: ကျေးဇူးတင်ပါတယ်။
ဒီဟိုတယ်ကောင်းပါတယ်နော်။
This hotel is nice, isn't it.
ဟုတ်ကဲ့၊ သိပ်ကောင်းပါတယ်။

vocab: ကျေးဇူးတင်ပါတယ်
ဟုတ်ကဲ့ခင်ဗျား

grammar.title: -ba- / -pa- — the politeness infix
grammar.explain: Slot -ba- (or -pa- after a syllable ending in -q) between the verb and -deh to make a statement polite. Pu-deh → Pu-ba-deh. This is the single most useful upgrade you can make to any sentence.
examples: ကောင်းပါတယ်

grammar.title: Théiq — "very"
grammar.explain: Place théiq directly before the verb to intensify it: théiq + kaun-ba-deh = "it's really good." Word order is reversed from English — the intensifier still comes before the verb, since the verb is always last.
examples: သိပ်ကောင်းပါတယ်

write: Same loop as က, with one extra hook curling off the top right. Draw က first, then add the hook without lifting your rhythm.
culture: Being offered a drink the moment you arrive somewhere isn't a special gesture — it's the default. Turning it down flat can read as more distant than intended. If you don't want anything, a soft ma-thauq-jin-ba-bú (Unit 3) plus a reason lands better than silence or a bare no, and it's completely normal to accept a small amount just to be polite even if you don't finish it.

name: ga
goal: Politely disagree about something everyday — like the weather, again.

lines: လက်ဖက်ရည်ရော။
ဟုတ်ကဲ့၊ သောက်ချင်ပါတယ်။

vocab: မကြိုက်ဘူး
လိုချင်တယ်
မလိုချင်ဘူး
နားမလည်ဘူး

grammar.title: ma-...-bú — the negative sandwich
grammar.explain: Burmese negates by sandwiching the verb: ma- goes on the front, -bú goes on the end, and the politeness infix -ba-/-pa- sits in between. Pu-deh becomes Ma-pu-ba-bú — never just "pu-deh + not."

grammar.title: Where ma- attaches on two-part verbs
grammar.explain: Some verbs are really two syllables glued together (like ná-leh-deh, "to understand"). The negative ma- goes before the second syllable, not the first: ná-ma-leh-ba-bú, not Ma-ná-leh-ba-bú.
examples: နားမလည်ဘူး

write: A closed loop with a small tail flicked off the base. Round the loop fully before you let the tail trail out to the right.
culture: A flat "no" is rarer in Burmese than the dictionary form suggests. Ma-...-bú is grammatically correct and genuinely used, but a lot of everyday refusal happens more softly — a reason instead of a refusal ("I'm full" rather than "I don't want it"), a hesitant laugh, or simply not answering directly. If someone seems to be dodging a clear yes/no from you, that hesitation often is the no.

name: ga (gha)
goal: Point at something and genuinely ask about it — without leading the listener toward an answer.

lines: မစားရသေးပါဘူး။
ဒါဆို ဒီဟာစားသလား။
ဟုတ်ကဲ့၊ စားပါတယ်။

vocab: ကြိုက်သလား

grammar.title: -tha-la / -dha-la — a genuine question
grammar.explain: Unlike -naw (Unit 1), which nudges the listener to agree, -tha-la (voiced to -dha-la after most syllables) is neutral — a real yes/no question with no expected answer either way. It's the natural way to ask about something you're actually unsure of, like whether a food is familiar to someone.
examples: ဒါစားသလား။

write: Two loops stacked — draw the lower loop first (like ဂ), then add the second loop directly above it.
culture: Pointing at food and asking "do you eat this?" is a genuinely common, welcome question from a visitor — it signals curiosity, not suspicion. If you're offered a taste of something unfamiliar, trying at least a small amount is read as warmth on your part, even if you don't finish it.

name: nga
goal: Count from one to ten, and use a classifier to ask how many people are in a group.

lines: မနက်စာဘယ်နှစ်ယောက်စားမလဲ။
နှစ်ယောက်ပါ။
ဟုတ်ကဲ့၊ ခဏလောက်စောင့်ပါ။
ကျေးဇူးတင်ပါတယ်။

grammar.title: Counting needs a classifier
grammar.explain: Burmese never counts a noun with a bare number — you always add a classifier (a counting word) after it. -yauq counts people: hna-yauq = "two (people)."

grammar.title: tiq, hniq, k'un-hniq weaken before a classifier
grammar.explain: "One," "two," and "seven" shorten their vowel to a. before most classifiers: tiq-yauq is never said — it's ta-yauq. Same for hniq → hna-, and k'un-hniq → k'un-na-.

write: A single hooked curve — no loop to close. One relaxed stroke, curling from top to bottom-left.
culture: Burmese hosts routinely over-cater — more food than the headcount needs is a quiet sign of generosity, not poor planning. If you're asked how many people are coming and you're unsure, rounding up is safer than rounding down.

name: sa (ca)
goal: Ask the price of something and understand the answer.

lines: ဒါဘယ်လောက်လဲ။
ငါးရာကျပ်ပါ။

vocab: ဈေးကြီးတယ်
ဈေးချိုတယ်
ဘယ်လောက်လဲ

grammar.title: beh-lauq-lé — asking a price or amount
grammar.explain: Beh-lauq literally means "how much" and takes the -lé question ending you'll formally meet in Unit 7. It's the single most useful phrase for shopping, taxis, and markets.
examples: ဒါဘယ်လောက်လဲ။

grammar.title: The Voicing Rule
grammar.explain: When two words join, the first consonant of the second word often "voices": s'eh ("ten") becomes -zeh in compounds like hna-s'eh (twenty, no change — after a˘) but thoun-zeh (thirty, s' voices to z). It doesn't happen after a syllable ending in -q.

write: Begins like a backward c, then flicks upward at the end. Practice the upward flick on its own before joining it to the curve.
culture: Bargaining is expected at a street market and basically absent at a fixed-price shop or supermarket — reading which kind of place you're in matters more than the specific words. A good-natured, smiling tone throughout the exchange is doing as much work as the numbers; treating it as a fight rather than a friendly back-and-forth is the actual foreign-tourist tell.

name: hsa
goal: Ask an open question using a question word instead of yes/no.

lines: ဒါထမင်းပါ။
ဟိုဟာက ဟင်းချိုပါ။

grammar.title: -lé — closing a question that already has a question word
grammar.explain: When your question already contains ba ("what"), beh-thu ("who"), or another question word, you close the sentence with -lé, not -tha-la. The two question endings are never mixed.

grammar.title: Question words stay in place
grammar.explain: Unlike English, Burmese doesn't move the question word to the front. Ba ("what") sits exactly where the answer word would go: Da ba-lé, literally "this what is?"

write: A loop with a small tail at the base. Draw the loop first, then anchor the tail underneath — like ဂ with an added foot.
culture: Asking what a dish is, and where it's from, is genuinely appreciated rather than seen as ignorant — Burmese cuisine varies a lot by region, and locals are often happy to explain. Complimenting a specific dish by name lands better than a generic "it's good."

name: za (ja)
goal: Say what you want, and turn any verb into a polite request.

lines: ဘာလိုချင်သလဲ။
ရေလိုချင်ပါတယ်။
ဟုတ်ကဲ့၊ ရပါတယ်။

vocab: လိုချင်တယ်

grammar.title: -jin-deh — "want to"
grammar.explain: Attach -jin-deh directly to a verb to mean "want to [verb]." Sa-jin-deh = "want to eat." It behaves exactly like any other -deh verb — it takes -ba-, -naw, -tha-la, and ma-...-bú normally.
examples: စားချင်တယ်
မစားချင်ဘူး

grammar.title: pé-ba — the all-purpose polite request
grammar.explain: Adding pé-ba ("give me," softened) after a verb turns it into a request: "please [verb] for me." You'll use this constantly — ordering food, asking for help, asking for the bill.
examples: ကူညီပေးပါ။

write: Echoes the shape of စ with a longer tail underneath. Write စ first, then extend the tail further down.
culture: You'll often be offered more of something right after you finish it, sometimes more than once, even after you've said you're full — it's closer to a ritual than a real question. A polite, firm ma-lo-ba-bú ("I don't need it") once or twice is normal and not rude; the offer isn't a test.

name: za (jha)
goal: Say you don't understand, and ask someone to repeat or slow down.

lines: ဆောရီး၊ နားမလည်ပါဘူး။
ကျေးဇူးတင်ပါတယ်။

vocab: နားမလည်ဘူး
အင်္ဂလိပ်လို
ဘယ်လိုပြောလဲ
နားလည်ပါတယ်

grammar.title: Loanwords slot in like native words
grammar.explain: Sáw-rí ("sorry") is a straight loan from English, but it takes Burmese grammar exactly like any native word — you can say Sáw-rí-naw or ask Sáw-rí-tha-la, though the plain form alone is what you'll use most.

grammar.title: Building requests with pé-ba
grammar.explain: P'yan-pyaw-pé-ba ("say again, please") and hné-hné pyaw-pé-ba ("speak slowly, please") both use the pé-ba pattern from Unit 8 — this is why that pattern is worth over-learning.

write: A less common letter today, mostly kept in older spellings. Recognize its shape — a loop with a low, extended tail — more than you'll write it.
culture: Struggling with fast, natural Burmese and asking someone to slow down is completely normal, not embarrassing — most people react with warmth or amusement, not impatience. A visitor making a genuine effort, mistakes included, is generally received far better than one who doesn't try at all.

name: nya
goal: Politely get a stranger's attention and understand their reply.

lines: ကို အောင် ပါ။ ကူညီပေးရမလား။
I'm Ko Aung. Should I help you?
ဟုတ်ကဲ့၊ ကျေးဇူးတင်ပါတယ်။
ဒီဟာဘယ်လောက်လဲလို့ မေးနေတာလား။
Were you asking how much this is?
ဟုတ်ကဲ့။ ဒီဟာဘယ်လောက်လဲ။

vocab: excuse me (to a man about your age)

grammar.title: Getting attention with kin terms
grammar.explain: Burmese doesn't have a neutral word for "excuse me" the way English does — instead you address a stranger with a kinship term that fits their approximate age and your gender relative to them: a-ma ("auntie") for an older woman, a-ko ("older brother") for a man near your age.

grammar.title: Gendered response particles
grammar.explain: Shin and bya both mean roughly "yes?" as a reply to being addressed — shin is used by and to women, bya by and to men. You'll hear both constantly in shops and cafés.

write: Sits low with a long curved tail beneath the line — give it plenty of room below the baseline before you start the next letter.
culture: Two things worth noticing here. First, addressing a stranger by a kinship term (a-ma for an older woman, a-ko for a man near your age — Unit 10's vocabulary) rather than a neutral "excuse me" is the actual norm, not an exception. Second, when you need to slip past someone in a crowded space, a slightly lowered head or shoulders while saying kwin-pyu-ba ("allow me") is a common physical gesture of respect, especially near elders or monks — making yourself briefly "smaller" as you pass is doing as much of the politeness as the words are.

name: ta
goal: Order food and drink at a café or restaurant.

lines: There's a café nearby. Shall we go?
မီနူးကြည့်လို့ရမလား။
ဟင်းချိုတစ်ခွက်ပေးပါ။
ဟုတ်ကဲ့၊ ခဏလောက်စောင့်ပါ။

vocab: ရေခဲမှုန့်

grammar.title: -lo ya-ma-la — "may I...?"
grammar.explain: Attach -lo ya-ma-la to a verb to ask permission — literally "if I [verb], will it be all right?" It's the standard way to ask "may I...?" or "can I...?" in any polite setting.
examples: ကြည့်လို့ရမလား။

grammar.title: Ordering with a classifier
grammar.explain: Just like counting people needs -yauq (Unit 5), ordering food needs the right classifier: -k'weq for a bowl or cup. Number + classifier + pé-ba is the whole pattern for ordering anything.
examples: တစ်ခွက်ပေးပါ။

write: A small loop with a flag-like stroke on top — one of the letters borrowed for Pali spellings; you'll meet it more in reading than writing.
culture: When a group of Burmese friends goes out to eat, there's often an unspoken understanding about who pays — frequently whoever is older, more established, or hosting. Ko Aung offering to cover the bill next unit isn't generosity out of nowhere; it's closer to a default expectation for him as the local, older friend.

name: hta
goal: Ask for the check and handle a simple payment.

lines: ဘေလ်ပေးပါ။
ငါးရာငါးဆယ်ပါ။
ဟုတ်ကဲ့၊ ဒါဆိုနောက်တစ်ခါ။
ကျေးဇူးတင်ပါတယ်။

vocab: ငွေလက်ခံသလား

grammar.title: Numbers keep stacking the same way
grammar.explain: 550 is ngá-ya-ngá-zeh — literally "5 hundred, 5 tens" — built exactly like the smaller numbers from Units 5–6, just chained together. No new grammar, only more digits.
examples: ငါးရာငါးဆယ်

grammar.title: da paq-hma — handing something over
grammar.explain: Da paq-hma ("here it is," literally "this — put — at") is what you say while physically handing over cash or an item. It pairs naturally with cé-zú-tin-ba-deh in reply.

write: Pairs with ဋ — another Pali-derived letter. Same small loop-and-flag shape, slightly rounder.
culture: Watch for the friendly "fight" over the bill — both people reaching for it, one insisting, the other protesting — it's a real, common social ritual, not awkwardness. Losing that fight gracefully (as Ko Aung does here, agreeing to "next time") is itself part of the etiquette.

name: da
goal: Tell a taxi driver where you're going and settle the fare.

lines: ကျွန်တော်တက္ကစီယာဉ်မောင်းတယ်။ ဘယ်ကိုသွားချင်လဲ။
I drive a taxi. Where do you want to go?
I want to go to Shwedagon Pagoda.
ဟုတ်ကဲ့။ လေးထောင်ကျပါတယ်။
That's a lot. A little discount, please?
ကျေးဇူးတင်ပါတယ်။

vocab: ဘယ်လောက်ကျလဲ

grammar.title: -go — marking where you're going
grammar.explain: Attach -go to a place name to mark it as your destination: [place]-go thwa-jin-ba-deh, "I want to go to [place]." This is the same -ko/-go you'll meet again in Unit 15 marking direct objects.
examples: ဈေးကိုသွားချင်ပါတယ်။
I want to go to the market.

grammar.title: Négotiating a price
grammar.explain: Théiq cí-ba-deh ("that's a lot") plus né-né shaw-pé-ba ("a little discount, please") is the standard two-line haggling exchange, using théiq from Unit 2 and pé-ba from Unit 8.
examples: သိပ်ကြီးပါတယ်။

write: A rounded loop with a hook trailing to the right — write the loop first, then let the hook flick out lightly.
culture: Most street taxis don't run on a meter — the fare is agreed before the ride starts, which is why Ko Aung states a price up front rather than waiting until arrival. Negotiating it isn't rude; not negotiating at all is what marks someone as unfamiliar with how it works.

name: da
goal: Guide a driver in real time — left, right, straight, and stop.

lines: တည့်တည့်သွားရမလား။
ရှေ့မှာဘယ်ဘက်ကိုလှည့်ပါ။
ဒီမှာရပ်ပါ။

grammar.title: Direction + -ko + verb
grammar.explain: Beh-beq-ko lé-ba is literally "left-side-to turn-please" — the same -ko direction marker from Unit 13's -go (they're the same marker; -ko after most syllables, -go after a nasal).
examples: ဘယ်ဘက်ကိုလှည့်ပါ။
ညာဘက်ကိုလှည့်ပါ။

grammar.title: Short, urgent imperatives
grammar.explain: In fast real-time situations like a moving taxi, Burmese drops down to bare verb + -ba, without the full -deh sentence — teh-teh thwa-ba, not the longer teh-teh thwa-ba-deh. Short and immediate.
examples: ဆက်သွားပါ။

write: A rarer letter today, close cousin of ဍ. Recognize it in older texts more than you'll need to write it.
culture: Giving directions from inside a moving vehicle is typically short and immediate — teh-teh thwa-ba ("go straight"), not a fuller polite sentence. The short imperative form isn't brusqueness, it's just what real-time, in-motion Burmese sounds like.

name: na
goal: Point at things and ask what they are and what they cost.

lines: ဘုရားဖူးပြီးရင် ဈေးလေးဝင်ကြည့်မလား။
After the pagoda, want to look at a little market?
ဟုတ်ကဲ့၊ ဝင်ကြည့်ရအောင်။
ဒါလုံချည်ပါ။
May I look at that one?
ရပါတယ်၊ ကြည့်ပါ။
ကျေးဇူးတင်ပါတယ်။

grammar.title: da / ho-da / di-ha — three ways to point
grammar.explain: Da is the all-purpose "this," ho-da specifically marks something farther away ("that, over there"), and di-ha adds emphasis ("this one right here"). All three work as the subject of a sentence exactly like any noun.
examples: ဟိုဒါဘာလဲ။

grammar.title: -ko marking an object
grammar.explain: When a verb acts on a specific, identified thing ("look at that one," not just "look"), the object takes -ko. It's optional with vague objects but expected with specific ones like ho-da.

write: This letter is Pali-only today — you'll recognize it in loanwords far more often than write it yourself.
culture: You're welcome to pick up and examine items at most stalls without any obligation to buy — handling goods is normal shopping behavior, not a commitment. A shopkeeper re-folding or replacing an item you looked at isn't a signal of annoyance.

name: ta
goal: Push back gently on a price and reach a number you're both happy with.

lines: ဒါဘယ်လောက်လဲ။
တစ်သောင်းပါ။
A little discount on the price, please.
မရပါဘူး၊ ဈေးဒီလောက်ပဲပါ။
Can't do it, the price is only this much.
Help him get a fair price.
ဒါဆို ရှစ်ထောင်ပါ။
ဟုတ်ကဲ့၊ ဝယ်မယ်။

grammar.title: -meh — the future/intention ending
grammar.explain: Weh-meh ("I'll buy it") uses -meh, the future counterpart to -deh: -deh states what is, -meh states what will be or what you intend. It follows the same politeness and negative patterns.

grammar.title: di-lauq-béh — "only this much"
grammar.explain: -béh ("only") attached to a quantity draws a firm line — a shopkeeper using it is signaling the price won't move further, politely but clearly.
examples: ဒီလောက်ပဲ။

write: One of the most common letters in the whole script: a flat top, a downstroke, a small foot. Worth drilling on its own before anything else.
culture: Bargaining among Burmese people is often closer to a friendly game than a confrontation — both sides know roughly where it'll land, and getting there with good humor matters as much as the final number. Having a local friend along, like Ko Aung here, commonly gets a better price than a visitor alone would — not through anything underhanded, just the ordinary "local rate."

name: hta
goal: Politely ask if you can take someone's photo.

lines: ဓာတ်ပုံရိုက်ချင်ပါတယ်။
I'd like to take a photo.
ရိုက်လို့ရမလား။
ရပါတယ်၊ ရိုက်ပါ။
ကျွန်တော် အတူတူရိုက်ပေးမယ်။
I'll take one of us together.
ကျေးဇူးတင်ပါတယ်၊ ကို အောင်။

grammar.title: Chaining -jin-deh and -lo ya-ma-la
grammar.explain: You can state your intention (Unit 8's -jin-deh: "I'd like to...") and then formally ask permission (Unit 11's -lo ya-ma-la: "may I?") back to back — very natural, very polite Burmese.
examples: ဓာတ်ပုံရိုက်ချင်ပါတယ်။ ရိုက်လို့ရမလား။
I'd like to take a photo. May I?

grammar.title: yaiq-pa — a short, warm "go ahead"
grammar.explain: The bare imperative yaiq-pa ("[go ahead and] take it") is friendlier and more immediate than a full -deh sentence — appropriate once permission is basically already given.

write: ထ is တ with a loop added on top. Write တ first, then curl the top stroke into a small loop.
culture: Always ask before photographing monks, at religious sites, or people in general — it's taken seriously, not a formality. The reverse also happens often: don't be surprised if locals ask to take a photo with you instead of the other way around, especially outside major cities.

name: da
goal: Ask for and follow directions to a place.

lines: နောက်တစ်နေရာ ဘယ်မှာလဲ။
တည့်တည့်သွားပါ။ ဘယ်ဘက်ကိုလှည့်ပါ။
ဒီလမ်းလား။
ဟုတ်ကဲ့၊ ဒီလမ်းပါ။
ကျွန်တော်ကိုယ်တိုင်လမ်းလျှောက်ချင်ပါတယ်။
I'd like to walk there myself.
Sure, I'll show you the way.
ကျေးဇူးတင်ပါတယ်။

vocab: to be far / to take long

grammar.title: -hma — marking location
grammar.explain: -hma attaches to a place or object to mark "at/in/on": Zé-hma = "at the market." It's also how you ask where something is: place-word + beh-hma-lé, "where is [place]?"
examples: ဈေးဘယ်မှာလဲ။
ဒီမှာရှိတယ်။

grammar.title: ca-deh doing double duty
grammar.explain: Ca-deh means both "to be far" and "to take a long time" — the same word covers physical and time distance, the way English sometimes overlaps "far" and "long."
examples: Is it far? / Will it take long?

write: A rounded loop with a flat base — a softer-edged cousin of တ.
culture: When you need to pass in front of someone — stepping past a seated group, cutting across someone's path — a small forward bow or lowered posture while moving through is the everyday version of "excuse me," often doing more work than any phrase. It's especially expected in front of elders or monks, but common enough generally that you'll see locals do it for each other too.

name: da
goal: Describe how close something is, using a nearby landmark.

lines: ဒီကနေ ဘယ်လောက်ကြာမလဲ။
ဆိုင်ဘေးမှာရှိတယ်။ ငါးမိနစ်ပဲ။
It's next to the shop. Just five minutes.
မကြာပါဘူး၊ နီးပါတယ်။

grammar.title: Landmark + -hma builds any location phrase
grammar.explain: The same -hma from Unit 18 turns any noun into a location word by combining with position words: s'ain-beq-hma ("next to the shop"), ta-da-nauq-hma ("behind the bridge"). Landmark first, position word, then -hma.

write: Takes ဒ and adds a small hook at the top-right corner — same base loop, one extra flick.
culture: Distance and time estimates in casual conversation are often more social than literal — "just a bit further" or "five minutes" can stretch a fair amount in practice. Treat these as reassurance more than precise measurement, the way you might in any language, just more so.

name: na
theme: Getting around by bus, car, or train
goal: Talk about how you're traveling and catch the right transport.

lines: ညနေဆို ဘယ်လိုပြန်ရမလဲ။
In the evening, how do I get back?
ဘတ်စ်ကားစီးလို့ရတယ်။ ဒါမှမဟုတ် တက္ကစီခေါ်လို့ရတယ်။
Baq-sa-ka si-lo ya-deh. Da-hma-ma-houq teq-ka-si k'aw-lo ya-deh.
You can take a bus, or call a taxi.
ဘူတာဘယ်လောက်ကြာလဲ။
ဒီကနေ ဆယ်မိနစ်ပဲ။
ဒါဆို ဘတ်စ်ကားစီးမယ်။
Okay, I'll be a phone call away.
ကျေးဇူးတင်ပါတယ်၊ ကို အောင်။

grammar.title: si-deh — the one verb for riding anything
grammar.explain: Si-deh covers riding a bus, car, train, bike, boat, or elephant — one all-purpose verb, unlike English's drive/ride/take. What changes is the noun in front of it, not the verb.
examples: ဘတ်စ်ကားစီးတယ်
ရထားစီးတယ်

grammar.title: si-ya-deh — "you catch it (there)"
grammar.explain: Adding -ya- before -deh signals possibility/necessity — roughly "[you] get to / need to [verb]." Si-ya-deh, "that's where you catch it," is subtly different from plain si-deh, "to ride."
examples: ဒီမှာစီးရတယ်။

write: One of the most frequent letters in the script — a loop with a straight tail down the right side.
culture: Strangers will often just point or physically walk a short distance with you to show the way, rather than give a verbal string of directions — showing is more common than telling. If someone starts walking alongside you after you ask directions, they're probably helping, not following you.

name: pa
goal: Answer the question every traveler gets asked first.

lines: ခဏနားရအောင်။ ဘယ်ကလာတာလဲ။
Let's rest a moment. Where do you come from?
အမေရိကန်ကလာပါတယ်။
မြန်မာကို ဘယ်တော့လာတာလဲ။
When did you come to Myanmar?
ဒီနှစ်ကလာပါတယ်။
ဒါဆို ပထမဆုံးလာတာပေါ့။
So this is your first time, then.
ဟုတ်ကဲ့၊ ပထမဆုံးပါ။
ကျေနပ်လား။
ဟုတ်ကဲ့၊ သိပ်ကျေနပ်ပါတယ်။

grammar.title: -ga — marking where from
grammar.explain: -ga attached to a place marks it as a source or starting point: Ameiq-ka-ga la-ba-deh, "I come from America." It pairs with beh-ga la-dha-lé? to ask and answer the same question.
examples: ဘယ်ကလာသလဲ။
အမေရိကန်ကလာပါတယ်။

write: A closed loop, flat-bottomed — this is the ပ from the very first example in the Basic Scripts Cheatsheet: ပ + ူ = ပူ.
culture: Personal questions that might feel forward elsewhere — where you're from, your age, whether you're married — are asked early and often in Myanmar, and answering them isn't an imposition, it's how people show interest in you. Expect this pattern to keep coming up through the rest of the book; it's not unique to Ko Aung.

name: hpa
goal: Talk about how long you're staying and what you think of the place.

lines: ဘယ်လောက်ကြာကြာနေမလဲ။
တစ်လပဲနေမယ်။
မြန်မာကို ဘယ်လိုထင်လဲ။
What do you think of Myanmar?
သိပ်လှပါတယ်။ လူတွေလည်း စိတ်ကောင်းကြတယ်။
It's really beautiful. And the people are kind, too.
ရွှေတိဂုံကို ဘယ်လိုထင်လဲ။
What did you think of Shwedagon?
အံ့သြစရာကောင်းတယ်။
ပြန်လာချင်သေးလား။
Do you want to come back again?
ဟုတ်ကဲ့၊ ပြန်လာချင်ပါတယ်။

vocab: စိတ်ဝင်စားတယ်
ပထမဆုံးအကြိမ်
ပြန်လာချင်တယ်

grammar.title: beh-lauq ca-ca — "for how long"
grammar.explain: Ca-ca (doubling ca-deh, "to take time") after beh-lauq asks specifically about duration, distinct from beh-lauq-lé (price, Unit 6) — same question word, different follow-up shapes the meaning.
examples: ဘယ်လောက်ကြာကြာနေမလဲ။

grammar.title: t'in-deh — sharing an opinion
grammar.explain: Beh-lo t'in-lé? ("what do you think?") is the natural opener for small talk about impressions — answer it with any adjective-verb you already know: hla-ba-deh, seiq-win-sa-ba-deh, kaun-ba-deh.
examples: ဘယ်လိုထင်လဲ။

write: ဖ is ပ with the top broken open into a loop. Write ပ, then let the top curl outward instead of closing.
culture: Warm, general praise of the country ("it's beautiful," "the food is great") is welcomed but sometimes lightly waved off, almost reflexively — a specific compliment about one place, dish, or person tends to land more genuinely than a broad one.

name: ba
goal: Introduce yourself and ask for someone else's name — properly, the Okell way.

lines: ဒါက ကျွန်တော့်သူငယ်ချင်း စု ပါ။
မင်္ဂလာပါ။ နာမည်ဘယ်လိုခေါ်သလဲ။
ကျွန်တော့်နာမည်က [name] ပါ။
တွေ့ရတာဝမ်းသာပါတယ်။
ကျွန်တော်လည်း တွေ့ရတာဝမ်းသာပါတယ်။
I'm glad to meet you too.
စုက ဒီမှာနေတဲ့ ကျွန်တော့်သူငယ်ချင်းပါ။
Su-ga di-hma né-deh ca-nawt thu-ngeh-jin ba.
Su's my friend who lives here.
ကို အောင်ရော ဘယ်လိုသိကြသလဲ။
And how do you two know each other?

vocab: ခင်ဗျား/ရှင်
you (to a man / to a woman, polite)

grammar.title: ca-na-w / ca-ma — "I", by speaker gender
grammar.explain: This is BAMA's own letter, and it starts the most personal sentence you'll learn: "I" has two words depending on who's speaking — ca-na-w for a man, ca-ma for a woman. Not a choice; it's fixed by the speaker's own gender.
examples: ကျွန်မကြိုက်ပါတယ်။

grammar.title: Nan-meh beh-lo k'aw-dha-lé — asking a name properly
grammar.explain: Literally "name — how — is called?" This is Okell's own phrasing for "what is your name?" — note k'aw-dha-lé uses the -tha-la/-dha-la question ending from Unit 4, closed by -lé because beh-lo is a question word (Unit 7's rule).
examples: နာမည်ဘယ်လိုခေါ်သလဲ။

write: ဗ — this is BAMA's own mark, and the first sound in ဗမာ, "Bama." A rounded top over a small loop underneath.
culture: Burmese names don't work like Western ones — there's no inherited family surname passed down, and a name is usually chosen fresh for each child, often tied to their birth day of the week astrologically. The title before a name (Ko, U, Daw, Ma — which you'll meet properly in later books) carries as much social information as the name itself.

name: ba
goal: Ask and answer questions about age.

lines: အသက်ဘယ်လောက်ရှိပြီလဲ။
ကို အောင်ကရော ဘယ်လောက်ရှိပြီလဲ။
And how old is Ko Aung?
ငါးဆယ်ရှိပါပြီ။
ငါကတော့ သုံးဆယ်ပဲ ရှိသေးတယ်။
စုက ငါ့ထက်အများကြီးငယ်တယ်။
Su's a lot younger than me.
None of us are the same age, huh.
ဟုတ်တယ်၊ ဒါပေမဲ့ သူငယ်ချင်းတွေပါ။
True, but we're friends all the same.

vocab: there is / to have / to be [age]
အသက်ကြီးတယ်
ငယ်ရွယ်တယ်

grammar.title: shi-deh — "there is," "to have," and age all at once
grammar.explain: Shi-deh is the general existence verb — "there is," "to have" — and Burmese states age with it: a-t'eq thoun-zeh-hniq shi-deh, literally "age thirty exists." It behaves like any other -deh verb for negatives and questions.
examples: အသက်ဘယ်လောက်ရှိပြီလဲ။
အသက်နှစ်ဆယ်ရှိပါတယ်။

grammar.title: -bi — a change that's already happened
grammar.explain: -bi replaces -deh when something has newly become true — shi-ba-bi ("[I] am now...") signals your age as an already-settled fact, not a general statement, subtly different from plain shi-ba-deh.
examples: နှစ်ဆယ်ရှိပါပြီ။

write: ဘ is a large open loop — one of the roomiest letters on the page. Give it space; don't let it collapse into a tight circle.
culture: Asking someone's age directly, as Su does here, is completely ordinary — age often determines the kinship terms and level of formality used with someone (whether you're a "Ko," older brother, or "younger" to them), so it's practical information, not a personal question the way it might read in English.

name: ma
goal: Talk about what you do for a living.

lines: ဘာအလုပ်လုပ်သလဲ။
ကျွန်တော် အင်ဂျင်နီယာလုပ်ပါတယ်။
ကျွန်မကတော့ ဆရာမလုပ်ပါတယ်။
ကျွန်တော်ကတော့ တက္ကစီယာဉ်မောင်းတယ်ဆိုတာ သိပြီးသားနော်။
You already know I drive a taxi, right.
အလုပ်ကြိုက်လား။

grammar.title: louq-teh — the general verb "to do"
grammar.explain: Louq-teh ("to do, to make") is the workhorse for describing any job: a-louq louq-teh ("to do work"), or noun + louq-teh ("to work as [noun]") — hsa-ya-ma louq-ba-deh, "I work as a teacher."
examples: ဆရာမလုပ်ပါတယ်။

write: Three humps in a row — a wave shape, evenly spaced. One of the easier letters to keep consistent at speed.
culture: Descriptions of one's own job often undersell it a little — modesty in talking about your own status or achievements is the norm, so a humble-sounding answer may reflect politeness more than the actual scale of what someone does.

name: ya
goal: Ask politely whether someone is married and reply about your own situation.

lines: ဟုတ်တယ်၊ ဇနီးရှိတယ်။
သားသမီးရှိသလား။
နှစ်ယောက်ရှိပါတယ်။
အားလုံးအခြေအနေမတူဘူးနော်။

grammar.title: shi-tha-la vs shi-bi-la
grammar.explain: Shi-tha-la (Unit 4's neutral question) simply asks "do you have?" Shi-bi-la adds -bi (Unit 24's change-of-state marker) — "are you [now, already]?" — the natural form for asking about marriage or age, since both describe a settled state.

write: A tall stroke with a loop at the base. Draw top to bottom first, then close the loop at the foot.
culture: Like age, marital status is asked early and directly — again, out of genuine social interest and because it shapes how people relate to you, not because it's considered private the way it might be elsewhere.

name: ya (ra)
goal: Talk about your parents and brothers and sisters, using the real kinship words.

lines: မောင်နှမရှိသလား။
အဖေအမေရှိသေးသလား။
ရှိသေးပါတယ်၊ ရွာမှာနေတယ်။
Still living, they live in the village.
ငါ့ကျတော့ အစ်ကိုတစ်ယောက်ပဲရှိတယ်။
I only have one older brother.
ရန်ကုန်မှာနေလား။
မဟုတ်ပါဘူး၊ မန္တလေးမှာနေတယ်။
Family's the most important thing, huh.

vocab: to still be alive / still there

grammar.title: -dhé — "still"
grammar.explain: Attach -dhé (voiced from -thé) before -deh to mean "still": shi-dhé-deh, "[they are] still there / still alive." A gentle, important suffix for asking about elderly relatives respectfully.
examples: ရှိသေးတယ်။
အလုပ်လုပ်နေသေးတယ်။

write: ရ curls in the opposite direction from ယ — same fluid energy, mirrored.
culture: Multi-generational households are common, and asking after someone's parents specifically is a real sign of respect and care, not small talk filler. Family is generally treated as the most stable, most important reference point in a conversation — you'll notice Ko Aung says as much outright in this unit.

name: la
goal: Say how you're feeling and keep a casual conversation moving.

lines: ဒီခရီးစဉ် ပျော်နေလား။
ပင်ပန်းနေသလား။
အနည်းငယ်ပင်ပန်းပါတယ်၊ ဒါပေမဲ့ ပျော်ပါတယ်။
A little tired, but I'm happy.
စိတ်ညစ်စရာရှိလား။
ကျေးဇူးတင်ပါတယ်၊ နှစ်ယောက်လုံး။

vocab: ပင်ပန်းတယ်
စိတ်ညစ်တယ်
စိတ်လှုပ်ရှားတယ်

grammar.title: -né-deh — happening right now
grammar.explain: Insert -né- before -deh to mark an action or state as continuous, in progress right now: pin-ban-né-deh, "[I] am tired [right now]," versus the timeless pin-ban-deh, "to be a tiring sort of thing."
examples: ပင်ပန်းနေတယ်။
အလုပ်လုပ်နေတယ်။

write: A single wide loop, low and rounded — one of the more forgiving letters to write at speed.
culture: Burmese conversation tends to keep an even, harmonious surface — genuine tiredness, stress, or worry is often understated ("a little tired" instead of "exhausted") rather than displayed openly. Reading past the understatement, and responding with the same gentle check-in Su does here, is more useful than taking the words at face value.

name: wa
goal: Suggest meeting up and check whether someone's free.

lines: မနက်ဖြန်အားလား။
ဟုတ်ကဲ့၊ အားပါတယ်။
ဒါဆို ညနေမှာတွေ့ကြရအောင်။
Then let's meet in the evening.
ဘယ်မှာတွေ့မလဲ။
Let's just meet at this café.
ဟုတ်ကဲ့၊ ရပါတယ်။
ဟုတ်ကဲ့၊ မနက်ဖြန်တွေ့မယ်။
မနက်ဖြန်တွေ့မယ်။

vocab: ဖုန်းခေါ်ပါ့မယ်

grammar.title: -ya-aun — a soft "let's"
grammar.explain: Twé-ca-ya-aun ("let's meet") uses -ya-aun on the verb — a gentle suggestion, not a command. It invites agreement the way -naw invites agreement on a statement, but on an action instead.
examples: စားရအောင်။

write: A simple, near-perfect circle — one continuous stroke, no corners.
culture: Two things worth knowing. On the phone, Burmese speakers commonly answer with Alo? (a loan from "hello," used only for phone calls — never in person). And on invitations: a specific plan with a place and rough time, like this unit's, is a real invitation meant to happen. A vaguer "come by sometime" offered in passing is often closer to warmth than a commitment — the way "we should get lunch sometime" often works in English. If you're not sure which one you've been given, it's completely fine to ask directly, or suggest a specific time yourself and see what happens.

name: tha (sa)
goal: Talk about the weather and what time it is.

lines: ရွာလိမ့်ပါတယ်၊ ညနေဆို။
အခုဘယ်နှစ်နာရီရှိပြီလဲ။
ဒါဆို မိုးမရွာခင် ပြန်ကြရအောင်။
Then let's head back before it rains.
ခုနက ပူတာနဲ့ အခုအေးသွားပြီနော်။
It was hot earlier, and now it's gotten cool, huh.
ဟုတ်တယ်၊ ရာသီဥတု အမြန်ပြောင်းတာပဲ။
True, the weather changes fast here.
မြန်မာမှာ ဒီလိုပါပဲ။
That's just how it is in Myanmar.

vocab: ပူအိုက်တယ်

grammar.title: Number + na-yi — telling time
grammar.explain: Just like counting people (Unit 5) or money (Unit 6), time uses a classifier: number + na-yi means "o'clock." Ngá-na-yi = "five o'clock," following the exact same number-classifier pattern you've used all book.

grammar.title: -lein — "looks like / seems"
grammar.explain: Ywa-lein-ba-deh ("looks like rain") uses -lein to soften a prediction — you're guessing based on evidence, not stating a fact outright.

write: A large loop with a tail curling under — a very common, distinctive shape you'll see everywhere in running text.
culture: Plans and daily rhythms often bend around the weather and the lunar calendar more than the clock — many holidays and events are set by the Buddhist calendar rather than a fixed Gregorian date. Treat scheduled times as reasonably loose by default, in both directions.

name: ha
goal: Get help fast when something goes wrong.

lines: ခေါင်းကိုက်နေတယ်။
ဘာဖြစ်လဲ။ နေမကောင်းဘူးလား။
What's wrong? Are you not feeling well?
ဟုတ်ကဲ့၊ နည်းနည်းမကောင်းဘူး။
I'll take you to the hospital.
ကျေးဇူးတင်ပါတယ်။
စိတ်မပူပါနဲ့၊ ကျွန်မတို့ ရှိတယ်။
narration: A short scare — a headache turns out to be nothing serious, but it's the moment you realize how far Ko Aung and Su are willing to go for a friend they've known less than a week.

vocab: to hurt / to be in pain

grammar.title: kaiq-teh — the go-to word for aches
grammar.explain: Body part + kaiq-teh ("to ache") covers almost any everyday pain: gaun kaiq-teh (headache), wun kaiq-teh (stomachache). Simple, high-frequency, and exactly what you need in an emergency.
examples: ခေါင်းကိုက်တယ်။
ဗိုက်ကိုက်တယ်။

grammar.title: t'wa-pé-ba — "please take (me)"
grammar.explain: T'wa-pé-ba ("please take/lead me there") combines with a place using -ko or -go: hsé-youn-go t'wa-pé-ba, or simply drop the marker in an urgent, clipped sentence, as above.
examples: Please take me to the hospital.

write: A tall loop with a straight leg down the right — write the loop first, then drop the leg without lifting the pen.
culture: What you're seeing in this unit — near-strangers dropping everything to help — isn't exaggerated for the story. A strong communal expectation to help someone in visible trouble, especially a guest, runs deep, and people will often go further than you'd think to ask for, or expect.

name: la (great)
goal: Apologize sincerely and accept an apology graciously.

lines: အနှောင့်အယှက်ဖြစ်စေလို့ တောင်းပန်ပါတယ်။
I'm sorry for the trouble I caused.
ကိစ္စမရှိပါဘူး။
သူငယ်ချင်းအချင်းချင်း ဒါလောက်တော့ လုပ်ရမှာပေါ့။
ကျွန်တော်တမင်မဟုတ်ပါဘူး။
It wasn't on purpose, of course.
သိပါတယ်၊ စိတ်မညစ်ပါနဲ့။
We know, don't worry about it.

vocab: တောင်းပန်တယ်
ခွင့်လွှတ်တယ်
ကိစ္စမရှိပါဘူး
နောက်တစ်ခါ
တမင်မဟုတ်ပါဘူး

grammar.title: A rare letter, a common courtesy
grammar.explain: ဠ appears in almost no modern words — it's kept mainly in Pali-derived spellings — but the phrase this unit teaches, taun-ban-ba-deh, is something you'll want ready in any language, any day.
examples: တောင်းပန်ပါတယ်။

write: Shares လ's loop with a small extra curl added. Write လ, then add the flourish without breaking stroke.
culture: Direct correction or confrontation in front of others is generally avoided in favor of a private, gentle word — public apologies or callouts can cause more embarrassment than the original problem. A quiet, sincere taun-ban-ba-deh, like Unit 32 teaches, usually closes the matter completely; there's rarely a need to revisit it.

name: a
goal: Close a conversation warmly, and look back at everything Book 1 covered.

lines: ပြန်တွေ့ကြမယ်။
တစ်ခါလာရင် ငါ့ဆီဆက်ခေါ်ပါ။
Whenever you come again, call me up.
Thank you so much, both of you.
Your Burmese has really improved, hasn't it.
ပထမနေ့ကနေ အခုထိ ကြည့်ပါ။
Look how far you've come since day one.
Thank you — it's thanks to both of you.
သွားလာပါဦးမယ်။
Take care — I'll be on my way too.
ကျန်းမာပါစေ။
narration: A month ago you landed in Yangon knowing four words. Today you're saying goodbye to two friends, in their language, without translating a single sentence in your head first.

vocab: နှုတ်ဆက်တယ်
ပြန်တွေ့မယ်
နှစ်ဆယ့်သုံး
တွေ့ရတာဝမ်းသာပါတယ်

grammar.title: The whole sentence engine, in one look back
grammar.explain: You've now met every consonant, and every core sentence-ending you need: -deh (state it), -naw (invite agreement), -ba-/-pa- (say it politely), ma-...-bú (say no), -tha-la/-dha-la (ask plainly), -lé (ask with a question word), -meh (say what will happen), -bi (say it's already so), and -né- (say it's happening right now).
examples: ပူတယ်။ ပူတယ်နော်။ ပူပါတယ်။ မပူပါဘူး။ ပူသလား။ ဘာလဲ။ ပူမယ်။ ပူပြီ။ ပူနေတယ်။
Pu-deh. Pu-deh-naw. Pu-ba-deh. Ma-pu-ba-bú. Pu-tha-la. Ba-lé. Pu-meh. Pu-bi. Pu-né-deh.
It's hot. Hot, isn't it? It's hot (polite). It's not hot. Is it hot? What is it? It'll be hot. It's (now) hot. It's (currently) hot.

write: အ stands alone — the only letter that's also a full vowel carrier by itself. A closed loop with a short tail, closing the set you opened in Unit 1.
culture: Burmese goodbyes tend to include a reciprocal blessing — kyan-ma-ba-zé ("stay well/healthy") rather than a bare "bye" — which is why Ko Aung closes with it here. And when a real friend says "call me next time you're here," as he does, it's almost always meant sincerely, not as a farewell formality — which is the real answer to a question from early in the book: how do you tell a genuine invitation from a polite one? By the time you reach here, you'll likely already know the difference by ear.
